title: Adobe's Project Indigo camera app adds Long Exposure mode for iPhone
summary: Adobe Project Indigo camera app adds long exposure mode for iPhone
detailed: Adobe updated its free experimental iOS camera app, Project Indigo, with a dedicated Long Exposure mode for merging multiple frames into a single virtual long exposure.

The new mode records up to 30 frames per second and offers 'Average' and 'Blend' processing styles for effects like motion-blurred water or light trails, supporting infinity frame captures that can exceed 1,000 frames.
The app is available for free on the App Store, requiring iPhone 12/13 Pro or iPhone 14 series or later running iOS 18.5+, with Adobe recommending an iPhone 15 Pro or later.

The release matters because it brings complex computational photography techniques—traditionally requiring slow mechanical shutters, physical neutral density filters, and dedicated cameras—directly to mobile devices.

Adobe has added a Long Exposure mode to Project Indigo, its free experimental camera app for iPhone.
It lets mobile photographers turn moving water into fog, car lights into glowing trails, and flashlights into patterns in the air.
Mobile cameras have small sensors, so image quality degrades quickly as exposures get longer.
On iPhones, a single exposure can last a second or so.
Longer shots, including the Night mode in the iPhone Camera app, combine several smaller frames.
Indigo’s new feature does the same, merging multiple frames into one virtual long exposure.
Indigo started in 2025 with a simple long exposure option within Night mode.
It’s now a separate mode, called Long, alongside Photo and Night.
The viewfinder shows a live preview as the exposure increases.
Users choose how many frames to capture.
The infinity setting allows for more than 1,000 frames, and the user manually stops the shot.
Indigo merges them into one of two styles.
Average takes the average of each frame.
Adobe says it’s good for waterfalls, waves, and fast-moving clouds, and can remove people or traffic from a busy scene.
Blend blends that average with the brightest value each pixel reached, so that short bursts of light don’t fade as the frame count increases.
Adobe says it’s good for car light trails, fireworks, lightning, and light painting.
Unlike Indigo’s Photo and Night modes, Long Exposure doesn’t align the frames before merging them.
The phone must remain completely still, ideally on a tripod.
“ Long Exposure isn’t meant for quick shots.
It works best for photos taken with deliberate intent,” Kainz and Levoy wrote.

Indigo records a maximum of 30 frames per second.
For light trails, the researchers advise a shutter speed slower than 1/30 second, otherwise the trails will appear blank.
On the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, Indigo can use the main lens with a variable aperture.
Switching from the default f/1.8 to f/2.8 or f/4.0 reduces light by a factor of 2.4 or 4.9.
For some shots, this removes the need for a neutral density filter.
The blog features light paintings made with the new feature by professional photographer Susan Magnano.
It also includes tips for shooting fireworks, steel, and lightning.
The feature was developed by Mohammad Haque and Yuting Yang with Adobe’s Nextcam team.
The researchers said they are looking at long handheld exposures, exposure bracketing, and photos of the Milky Way on moonless nights.
Indigo is free on the App Store.
It works on iPhone 12 and 13 Pro models and any iPhone 14 series or later with iOS 18.5 or later.
Adobe recommends an iPhone 15 Pro or later.
Users can also open it from within Lightroom Mobile via the Tech Preview setting.
The previous update to Indigo added an AI playground for photo editing.
Levoy led work on the cameras on Google’s Pixel phones before joining Adobe.
On the community forum, the Indigo team says that handheld shooting isn't yet supported in Long Exposure mode.
Attempts at handheld light shots proved the point: both styles require a phone that doesn't move at all, and some trial and error.
Still, I was impressed, in a slightly odd way.
On a dedicated camera, effects like these require a slow shutter, careful metering, and often an ND filter.
Indigo creates them from a stack of frames and shows the image forming in the viewfinder, much like Live Composite does on OM System cameras and Live View Composite does on some Panasonic models.
